newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Britain's Cook seeks tailored EU accession plans.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Cook seeks tailored EU accession plans.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told Czechs on Wednesday that London would seek separate "tailor-made" programmes to prepare each Central European candidate for European Union membership.

Writing in the largest Czech daily, Mlada Fronta Dnes, Cook said Britain would seek to launch accession talks with the five countries recommended last month by the European Commission when it takes over the EU's rotating presidency in January.

"I am determined to secure a decision at (the EU's summit in) Luxembourg in December which allows us to open a negotiating process during the UK's presidency of the EU, beginning with those applicants which are most ready," he said.

On July 15, the Commission recommended opening accession talks with former communist Poland, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia and the Czech Republic as well as Cyprus, but the final decision on whom to invite is left to the member states.
The recommendation was for the 15-nation EU to start membership talks in early 1998, saying that the five may become members in four to six years' time.
Cook wrote in Mlada Fronta Dnes that the EU should offer "solid practical help" to prepare new members.
"I want to see tailor-made programmes for each country so that the Central European candidates can work towards joining the Union as soon as they, and the Union itself, are ready."
Analysts say even the front-runners among the 10 applicants from central and eastern Europe face an uphill struggle.

The five chosen countries could increase the EU's population by about 17 percent to more than 430 million , but have a combined gross domestic product equal to only 6.1 percent of the EU, or 391 billion ECU.

Leaders of the EU failed at their Amsterdam summit in June to find agreement on the sensitive issue of dividing power and influence within its decision-making institutions -- a prerequisite to any further expansion.
Before enlargement the EU also must agree to reform costly agricultural and regional support policies.
Cook backed the proposal to cap the total EU budget at 1.27 percent of the Union's gross national product.
"This will provide adequate funds for effective Community action even in an enlarged EU," Cook wrote in the Czech paper.

"This means that all existing member states will have to accept a lower level of receipts in the next century. The important point is that the future arrangements should be affordable, efficient, durable and fair," he added.
Cook referred only to "Central European" countries in his article and said: "This issue is not whether all the Central European countries will join, but when and on what terms."
The commission, and analysts, agree that Hungary and Poland are closest to satisfying membership conditions and the Czech Republic and Slovenia are not far behind.

Estonia, the only Baltic state picked, has furthest to go, and those left out of the recommendations -- Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Latvia and Lithunania, have vowed to press on with their quest for EU membership.

"Tragically, Central Europe was denied the opportunity to play its part in the project of European partnership. But now for the first time in its history, the Union has a real chance to speak for the greater part of Europe," Cook said. REUTER
